name: libhat
baseline: std::search (MSVC STL; byte-pattern search in a random buffer)
workload: Single-threaded search for a 9-byte pattern (01 02 .. 09) that never matches in a seeded random buffer of 4 MiB to 256 MiB, Google Benchmark, real time, 4 s minimum per run, libhat AVX2 scanner without scan hints.
claimed_speedup: libhat+AVX2 55.1129 GiB/s at 4 MiB and 23.3351 GiB/s at 256 MiB versus std::search 2.89578 GiB/s and 2.89598 GiB/s (about 19x and about 8.1x, derived from page data); the two other pattern scanners in the table reach 2.29 GiB/s (csgosimple) and about 0.96 GiB/s (learn_more).
compiler_and_flags: clang-cl 22.1.1 with the MSVC 14.51.36231 toolchain on Windows, default release flags /GR /EHsc /MD /O2 /Ob2 (README); benchmark source test/benchmark/Compare.cpp read via raw.githubusercontent.com
stars_or_usage: 148 stars; vcpkg port 'libhat' in the vcpkg ports list
tradeoffs: Scanner needs SSE4.1 or AVX2 (x86), AVX-512 (x86-64) or NEON (ARM) for the vector paths, with runtime cpuid validation; patterns are IDA-style byte signatures with wildcards, not general string search. Optional x86_64/aarch64 scan hints trade a small data table for faster scans of machine code. C++20; bindings for C, Java, Python and C#. Aimed at game hacking in user space (signature scanning, memory protection helpers).
caveats: First-party benchmark. The baseline is std::search on the MSVC STL; its flat 2.9 GiB/s at every size looks like a scalar path, but the README does not say how std::search was invoked or whether any vectorised STL path applied, so the 8x to 19x gap may shrink against a tuned memchr-style search. 4 MiB to 16 MiB sizes fit in cache and drop from 55 to 23 GiB/s once the buffer leaves L2/L3. The needle has no wildcards and never matches (worst case for the scan). Only one CPU and one compiler were used.
found_via: vcpkg ports list (raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/vcpkg/master/versions/baseline.json) showed port 'libhat'; its README Benchmarks section was then read

name: camellia-simd-aesni
baseline: Camellia reference implementation (NTT camellia-BSD-1.2.0 camellia.c, table-based scalar C, built at -O2 in the same harness)
workload: Camellia-128 encryption/decryption throughput in MiB/s from the repo's own test harness main.c, SIMD implementations processing 16 or 32 blocks in parallel versus the reference doing one block at a time.
claimed_speedup: SIMD256 32-block intrinsics, AVX512+GFNI: ~18.7x on Ryzen 9 7900X, ~17.8x on Core i3-1115G4, ~14.1x on Ryzen 9 9950X3D; AVX2+AES-NI: ~5.4x (Core i5-6500). SIMD128 16-block: ~3.1x to 4.5x on x86, ~2.2x to 3.0x on ARM and POWER9. README sample output (Ryzen 9 7900X): reference 372.041 MiB/s versus asm SIMD256 5159.460 MiB/s (about 13.9x, derived from page data). The 1-block SIMD128 variants are slower than the reference (for example 238.747 vs 372.041 MiB/s).
compiler_and_flags: GCC -O2 with per-target -march flags given in the README build log (sandybridge/haswell/znver4 plus -maes -mvaes -mgfni -mavx512*); individual rows cite gcc-13, gcc-14 or gcc-15; harness is main.c and the reference is camellia-BSD-1.2.0/camellia.c in the repo
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 7900X (Zen 4), Ryzen 9 9950X3D (Zen 5), Intel Core i3-1115G4, Core i5-6500, ARM ThunderX2, Cortex-A53 (648 MHz), POWER9
tradeoffs: Only pays when 16 or 32 blocks are available in parallel (CTR, CBC decrypt, CFB decrypt, XTS, OCB); not useful for CBC encryption or single blocks. Needs AES-NI/VAES/GFNI with AVX2 or AVX-512 on x86, ARMv8 Crypto Extension on AArch64, VSX plus AES on POWER, or RVA23 Zvkb+Zvkned on RISC-V. Hand-written GAS assembly files and C intrinsics; targets one cipher, not a general SIMD library. The README presents a constant-time alternative to table lookups.
caveats: First-party numbers. The reference is a table-based implementation compiled at -O2, not an optimised library such as libgcrypt or OpenSSL assembly (the README calls it the OpenSSL reference). Best-case ratios (18.7x) need GFNI on AVX-512 hardware; the 1-block SIMD128 variants are 1.2x to 2.9x slower than the reference on most listed CPUs (one 1.2x faster case), as the README admits. Last commit date taken from the commits page.
found_via: WebSearch 'vcpkg port SIMD accelerated library x86 AVX2 NEON faster than scalar' snippet naming jkivilin/camellia-simd-aesni, then README and repository pages opened

name: corvus
baseline: scalar vendor libm called through std::cos/std::sin/std::exp/std::lgamma (UCRT on Windows, Apple libSystem on macOS); also compared against corvus's own element-at-a-time calls
workload: Element throughput (ns per element) of SIMD-vectorised double-precision erf, lgamma, exp, log, log1p, cos, sin over n = 10^6 seeded inputs, median of repeated timings after warm-up, on a quiet machine gated at 5% ambient CPU.
claimed_speedup: cos/sin 5.50x/5.58x over UCRT on Ryzen 7 (Zen 4, 1.6 ns/el), 4.87x/4.98x over Apple x86 libm on Kaby Lake (4.4 ns/el), 3.27x/3.21x over Apple arm64 libm on M1 (single gated run, flagged 'reported, not published'); exp 1.20x (Zen 4); lgamma 1.5x to 5.2x against UCRT but 0.2x to 0.9x against Apple libm; log 0.64x, 0.27x, 0.21x and log1p 0.92x, 0.40x, 0.32x (slower than libm).
compiler_and_flags: clang-cl Release (Zen 4, Windows 11) and Apple Clang 15 Release with the 'release' preset and Ninja (Kaby Lake, macOS 13.7); harness tools/quiet_bench.ps1 with raw evidence under docs/bench-evidence
hardware: Ryzen 7 (Zen 4, AVX3_ZEN4 tier), Intel i7-7820HQ (Kaby Lake, AVX2), Mac Mini M1 (NEON)
stars_or_usage: 1 star; built on Highway for dispatch
tradeoffs: Accuracy-first double-precision kernels (about 1 ULP bounds, validated against an mpmath oracle) that carry double-double intermediates, so the README states that throughput is not the claim. Needs array-style batch calls; advantage is close to none at two lanes. Highway (Apache-2.0) is distributed with binaries. Covers statistical special functions (erf/erfc, lgamma, incomplete gamma and beta and inverses, Bessel I0/I1) plus an elementary family.
caveats: Wins are function specific: sin and cos only, while log and log1p are slower than every vendor libm measured by design, and lgamma is faster than UCRT but slower than Apple's libm. The libm baseline matters more than the kernel (the document says so); glibc and MSVC-compiled builds were not measured, only clang-cl and Apple Clang. The PERFORMANCE document lists two families as not yet reproducible and the M1 elementary column as indicative only. A 1-star, very new repository maintained by one author.
found_via: github.com/topics/simd?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=updated listing (recently updated C++ SIMD repos), then README and docs/PERFORMANCE.md read

name: Vectis
baseline: scalar C++ loop (and the same loop with four independent accumulators, and the same loop built with -ffast-math), as the reference for an AVX2 intrinsics/assembly dot-product kernel
workload: dot_f32 over n = 1024 floats, L1-resident, min of 21 runs, comparing scalar, scalar-4acc, intrinsics and hand-written GAS assembly twins with the same shape.
claimed_speedup: scalar 1491 ns (4.92 cycles/element) versus intrinsics 107 ns (0.338 cycles/element, 13.93x) and assembly 107 ns (0.333 cycles/element, 13.93x); scalar with four accumulators 679 ns (2.05x), so the vector code is about 6.3x faster than the fairer scalar loop (derived from page data); the naive loop built with -ffast-math reaches 6.9x. saxpy at n = 1024: assembly 100 ns versus intrinsics 132 ns (1.28x).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 15.2/16 per the README test matrix; Release build with VECTIS_ISA_TIER=avx2 meaning -march=x86-64-v3 -mno-avx512*; bench/bench_asm.cpp uses min of 21 runs and rdtsc cycles per element (file read through GitHub, it states no flags itself)
hardware: Intel i5-6500T (Skylake, AVX2, FMA, no AVX-512), 32 KiB L1d, powersave governor
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20/23 vec<T,N> over scalar, AVX2 and AVX-512 backends; no SSE4 tier, no NEON; consumer must pass -march (otherwise the scalar backend is selected). Optional GAS assembly layer (dot, saxpy, sum) that the README itself recommends not adding by default. AoS to SoA with C++26 reflection needs GCC 16 -freflection.
caveats: Brand-new single-author repository (first commit 2026-09-20). The 13.9x figure is mostly summation order and FMA, not vector width, which the README says itself (scalar-4acc already gives 2.05x). Only AVX2 is measured; AVX-512 is compiled but never benchmarked, and the latest commit message says it fixed false AVX-512 claims. Benchmark compiler is inferred from the README test matrix. SoA conversion is slower than AoS above L2-size working sets.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com only) 'AVX2 header-only C++ library faster than STL std::find std::count std::accumulate SIMD README speedup table github' returned Vectis; README and commits page opened

name: SSW (Complete-Striped-Smith-Waterman-Library)
workload: Smith-Waterman alignment of 1000 Ion Torrent E. coli reads (about 25 to 540 bp) against the 4,938,920-nucleotide E. coli 536 reference using SIMD striped scoring; the README gives CPU time for SSW only.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Current version of our implementation is ~50 times faster than an ordinary Smith-Waterman.' Absolute CPU time for the E. coli test: AMD CPU about 880 s (default penalties) or about 460 s (-m1 -x3 -o5 -e2); Intel CPU about 960 s or about 500 s; about 40 MB memory.
stars_or_usage: 323 stars, 119 forks; packaged in Debian as libssw
tradeoffs: C API with a C++ wrapper (also Python, Java and R wrappers); integer penalties only, small penalty values recommended for shorter run time; returns score, location and CIGAR for the optimal alignment and heuristic sub-optimal score. Uses SIMD instructions (the README page does not name the instruction set).
caveats: The '~50 times' headline names no comparison program, data or hardware on the page, and the CPU-time figures have no baseline column. The README cites a PLoS ONE paper (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0082138) for the method, which was not opened because doi.org is blocked here. Benchmark compiler and flags are not stated.
found_via: Recalled while checking SIMD sequence-alignment libraries (parasail, SSW) against the vcpkg ports list; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com and GitHub pages

name: FastArrayOps
baseline: best compiler output and STL scalar loops (std::find, std::min_element, std::max_element, index of min/max)
workload: AVX2 contains/find, min/max element and min/max index over arrays of I8/U8 to I64/U64, float and double, large n; the README says proportional speedup is higher for small n.
claimed_speedup: README table 'Approx. speedup vs. best compiler output' for large n: contains/find 22x (I8/U8), 18x (I16/U16), 12x (I32/U32), 7.0x (I64/U64), 13.0x (float), 7.0x (double); min/max element 2.3x, 2.1x, 1.1x, 1.3x, 28x (float), 14x (double); min/max index 35x, 19x, 8.5x, 3.1x, 8.9x, 5.0x. Headline: 'up to 35x faster than compiler or STL'.
tradeoffs: x86 AVX2 only; single header fast-array-ops.h with Linux and Windows build folders. Min/max index does not say which index is returned among equal minima; find-element does return the lowest index; empty arrays and not-found return ~0U/~0ULL. The README argues linear scans beat hash tables or heaps up to hundreds or thousands of elements.
caveats: First-party table with no CPU, compiler, flags, array sizes or timing method stated, and the 'best compiler output' baseline is not identified. Several rows are small (min/max element for 32-bit integers 1.1x, 64-bit 1.3x). The Linux/ and Windows/ folders were not opened, so whether they hold the benchmark driver is unconfirmed. Last commit (2025-12-11) is a bugfix to FastFind64 and FastIdx16, so older numbers may predate it.
found_via: github.com/topics/avx2?l=c%2B%2B listing led to the komrad36 profile (github.com/komrad36?tab=repositories), whose FastArrayOps README was read

name: Leftpack (komrad36)
baseline: naive scalar left-pack loop (branchy, 'super naive') and branchless naive scalar loop, both listed in the README
workload: AVX2 left-pack (compress): keep the elements selected by a bitmask and write them contiguously, for 8-, 16-, 32- and 64-bit elements.
claimed_speedup: README 'Approx. speedup vs. naive methods': 8-bit 39x versus super naive and 5.3x versus branchless naive; 16-bit 31x and 3.8x; 32-bit 14x and 2.2x; 64-bit 7.8x and 1.6x. README also says it beats the AVX-512 VCOMPRESS instructions for the bitmask case (no number given).
compiler_and_flags: README: supports clang, gcc and MSVC and tests were run on all three; no flags stated
tradeoffs: x86 AVX2 (8-bit and 32-bit versions use BMI2 PDEP/PEXT, very slow on AMD Zen 1 and Zen 2, so alternative slightly slower implementations are provided); header leftpack.h with test.cpp.
caveats: First-party table with no CPU, compiler, flags or sizes stated, and the VCOMPRESS comparison has no numbers. The 'super naive' baseline is a branchy loop that mispredicts on random masks, so the 39x end flatters the result; the branchless loop (1.6x to 5.3x) is the fairer scalar baseline. Last commit three years and one week before the run date.
found_via: komrad36 profile page (github.com/komrad36?tab=repositories) reached from github.com/topics/avx2?l=c%2B%2B; README read

name: FastDivide (komrad36)
baseline: hardware 64-bit unsigned div instruction (what a runtime a / b and a % b compile to on x86-64)
workload: 64-bit unsigned integer division and modulo of arbitrary runtime operands, plus an optional precomputed-divisor class for repeated division by the same divisor.
claimed_speedup: README: 'About 30% faster' than the hardware div instruction, 'at least on Intel, where div is crazy slow'; no timing table is given.
compiler_and_flags: README: supports Clang, GCC and MSVC; no flags stated
tradeoffs: Scalar branchless algorithm (leading-zero count, shifts and five Newton-Raphson iterations, then a multiply-high), not SIMD, so it is a weak fit for this category; uses more registers than a single div, so spills can erase the win; undefined for division by zero; no side-channel leakage via branches or memory. For divisors known at compile time the compiler is better. Single header fast-divide.h.
caveats: Only a prose claim; no benchmark source, numbers, CPU model or compiler version on the page, and the README itself limits the claim to Intel, where it says div is slow, so results on cores with a faster divider may differ. Last commit is a README edit.
found_via: komrad36 profile page (github.com/komrad36?tab=repositories) reached from github.com/topics/avx2?l=c%2B%2B; README read

name: FastDivide128 (komrad36)
baseline: compiler-rt __udivti3, __umodti3 and __udivmodti4 (unsigned 128-bit division as lowered by Clang)
workload: Unsigned 128-bit integer Div, Mod and DivMod on x86 Haswell or newer.
claimed_speedup: README: 'about 2x faster than the compiler-rt stuff'; no timing table is given.
compiler_and_flags: README: primarily Clang (inline assembly where codegen was poor); compiles under GCC with worse code; no flags stated
hardware: x86 Haswell or newer (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Written to fill the missing __udivti3 on Windows/Clang; uses inline assembly, so Clang-first and x86 Haswell+ only; one header plus fast-div-128.cpp; not for compile-time operands. Not SIMD, so a weak category fit.
caveats: Prose claim only: no benchmark source, numbers, CPU or compiler version. The baseline is the generic compiler-rt routine rather than a tuned library such as libdivide or GMP.
found_via: komrad36 profile page 2 (github.com/komrad36?page=2&tab=repositories) reached from github.com/topics/avx2?l=c%2B%2B; README read

name: KFAST
baseline: Rosten's reference FAST corner detector (shipped in the repo's Rosten folder) and OpenCV's FAST implementation, both in the test driver
workload: FAST feature-detector corner detection with optional non-maximal suppression on test images (results.jpg and test.jpg), single-threaded and multi-threaded.
claimed_speedup: README: 'outperforms the next-fastest implementation by 60% single-threaded or 500% multi-threaded (!) while exactly matching its output'; the header comment in main.cpp says 'outperforms the reference implementation by 40-60% single-threaded or 500% multi-threaded'. The bar chart (results.jpg) holds the actual timings and was not readable.
compiler_and_flags: Linux g++ via the repo Makefile, Windows MSVC, C++11 or newer; flags not stated
tradeoffs: Single header KFAST.h with no dependencies; needs AVX2; multithreaded; output claimed bit-identical to the reference. The test driver needs OpenCV for the comparison and image loading. Bundles Rosten's BSD-licensed reference code.
caveats: Speedup percentages are first-party and the 'next-fastest implementation' is not named in the text, while the driver comment says the reference implementation; the multi-threaded 500% presumably compares threads to one thread, which is not stated. No CPU or compiler flags on the page. Last code changes date from 2016 to 2019; the 2021 commit only adds a LICENSE file.
found_via: komrad36 profile page (github.com/komrad36?tab=repositories) reached from github.com/topics/avx2?l=c%2B%2B; README and main.cpp header read

name: qAverageColor
baseline: serial scalar per-channel sum loop for the average color of an RGBA8 image (the 'Serial' column in the repo README)
workload: Average color of a synthetic 10-megapixel RGBA8 image using psadbw-based SSE4.2, AVX2 and AVX-512 accumulation versus the serial loop.
tradeoffs: x86 only (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512 variants selected at build time); the accumulators are 64-bit and overflow-safe; mostly a teaching write-up with source under include/ and source/.
caveats: First-party and old (last commit 2021, GCC 8.2.1); build flags are not stated, so the serial baseline may or may not have been auto-vectorised by the compiler. The repo has a tests folder that was not opened, so the benchmark program is unconfirmed. Modest (2x to 6x) gains for a memory-bound sum.
found_via: Wunkolo profile page (github.com/Wunkolo?tab=repositories&sort=stargazers), looked up while reviewing small SIMD study repos; README read

name: PTMS (Parallel Tournament Merge Sort)
workload: Sorting 4 million ints (16 MB, cache-resident) with OpenMP tasks, parallel merging and AVX2/AVX-512 bitonic base cases at 16 threads.
claimed_speedup: Median seconds: std::sort 0.300 (1.00x), tbb::parallel_sort 0.036 (8.30x), PTMS 0.0163 (about 18.4x versus std::sort; about 2.2x versus tbb::parallel_sort, derived from page data). On a Ryzen 7 7500F with AVX-512: median 0.0162 s at 12 threads.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build, C++17, OpenMP 4.5+; compiler version and flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 6900HX (16 threads); AMD Ryzen 7 7500F (AVX-512, 12 threads)
tradeoffs: Int (sort_int) only, needs a caller-supplied scratch buffer, OpenMP tasks (MSVC needs clang-cl), AVX2 or AVX-512 base cases selectable with -DSIMD; benchmark program in the benchmark/ folder.
caveats: Headline 18.4x compares 16 threads with one-thread std::sort, so the like-for-like result is the 2.2x over tbb::parallel_sort. One size (4M random ints, cache-resident) and one CPU model per number; compiler flags unstated; brand-new repository with no external verification. It is a sorting algorithm more than a SIMD library, filed here because the base cases are SIMD networks.
found_via: github.com/topics/avx2?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=updated listing (recently updated C++ AVX2 repos), README opened
